claims.text: Adding approximately 3 at.% Nb during melt-casting will produce fine, coherent Nb-rich nanoprecipitates in a MnNiSi-based alloy.
The Nb-rich nanoprecipitates will preferentially be dispersed along MnNiSi grain boundaries.
Homogenization at approximately 900°C for 12 hours followed by rapid quenching will generate the proposed precipitate structure.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can substantially strengthen a magnetic alloy.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can improve strength while retaining ductility.
Secondary-phase precipitation can increase hardness by affecting dislocation mobility.
The proposed Nb-rich precipitates will produce precipitation hardening in MnNiSi.
The Nb-rich nanoprecipitates will deflect cracks.
The Nb-rich nanoprecipitates will facilitate dislocation motion.
High precipitate–matrix coherency minimizes lattice distortion fields relevant to magnetic domain-wall motion.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can enhance mechanical properties without sacrificing soft-magnetic performance.
Minimizing distortion through precipitate coherency will preserve the magneto-structural coupling responsible for the magnetocaloric effect in MnNiSi.
The 3 at.% Nb alloy will have greater tensile strength than the similarly processed Nb-free baseline.
The 3 at.% Nb alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the similarly processed Nb-free baseline.
The 3 at.% Nb alloy will retain a magnetic entropy change comparable to that of the Nb-free baseline.
The predicted combination of mechanical and magnetocaloric performance requires strict maintenance of the stated casting, homogenization, and quenching conditions.
Excess Nb or processing deviations may produce larger, incoherent precipitates.
Larger, incoherent precipitates may adversely affect the magnetocaloric properties of MnNiSi.

contradictions.description: The proposed precipitation-hardening explanation says the precipitates facilitate dislocation motion, whereas strengthening by coherent precipitates is ordinarily framed here, and in the cited evidence, as impeding dislocation motion. This weakens the stated causal explanation for increased tensile strength.
